lines.text: Inside a four cylinder engine at three thousand revs, a hundred explosions go off every second. And you feel none of them. To see how, we have to cut one open.
This is a heavy metal block, with round tubes bored straight through it. Those are the cylinders. Inside each one, a piston. A metal plug that slides up and down, sealed by thin springy rings.
Underneath, a connecting rod links the piston to the crankshaft. Push the piston down, and the crank swings round. Just like your leg pushing a bicycle pedal.

On top sits the head. Two little doors, called valves. One lets air in, one lets exhaust out. A spinning camshaft pushes them open, and springs snap them shut. And right in the middle, the spark plug.
Now watch one cycle, slowed right down. Stroke one. Intake. The piston slides down, the intake valve opens, and it sucks in air, with a fine mist of fuel.
Stroke two. Compression. Both valves shut. The piston rises, and squeezes that mixture into about a tenth of the space.

Stroke three. Power! The plug fires a spark of over twenty thousand volts. The mixture burns in a flash, hotter than two thousand degrees. The gas expands, and slams the piston down with the force of a few tonnes.
Stroke four. Exhaust. The exhaust valve opens, and the piston shoves the burnt gas out, towards your tailpipe. Then it all starts again.
Four strokes. Two full turns of the crankshaft. And only one of them makes power. So why doesn't the car jerk?
Because four cylinders take turns. One, three, four, two. While one fires, the others are breathing in, squeezing, and breathing out. There's always a piston pushing.
A heavy flywheel on the end smooths out the rest. And the crank sends that spin through the gearbox, to your wheels.
Now speed it up. At three thousand revs, every piston stops dead and reverses a hundred times a second. Each cylinder fires twenty five times a second.
And here's the strange part. Most of the fuel never moves you at all. Roughly two thirds of its energy escapes as heat, out of the exhaust and the radiator.
Nikolaus Otto built the first working four stroke engine in eighteen seventy six. Nearly a hundred and fifty years later, most petrol cars still run on his idea.
An engine never pushes in one giant bang. It splits the work, and fires in turns. Orbi Transfer sends big videos the same way.
Drop in a video, up to twenty gigabytes. Orbi cuts it into parts, and sends three at once. If your signal drops, it carries on where it stopped.
Send it from your phone, open it on your laptop. No login, no app, just a browser. It's locked on your phone before it leaves. And after thirty minutes, it burns.
Orbi Transfer dot com. A hundred explosions a second, and you never felt one.
